description: The eternal inner self (atman), the cycle of birth and death (samsara), the law of karma and liberation (moksha).
content_html:
The Eternal Inner Self: Atman

At the centre of Hindu teachings about human nature is the concept of atman. The Upanishads teach that every living being has an atman — an eternal, unchanging inner self that is quite distinct from the physical body and even the mental personality. The body ages and dies; the mind changes mood and opinion; but the atman is permanent.

The Bhagavad Gita describes the atman as indestructible: it cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, wetted by water or dried by wind. This teaching gives Hindu understanding of death a distinctive character: what is called death is really the departure of the atman from one physical body. The atman itself never dies.

Different Hindu schools understand the relationship between atman and Brahman differently. In Advaita Vedanta (associated with Shankara), atman and Brahman are ultimately one — liberation means realising this identity. In Vishishtadvaita (associated with Ramanuja), atman is real but distinct from God — the individual soul is a part of Brahman, as the body is a part of the self. In Dvaita (associated with Madhva), atman and Brahman are eternally distinct but the soul depends entirely on Brahman. These variations matter on the GCSE, because top-band answers name the sub-tradition.

Key Fact

Atman = the eternal inner self, distinct from the body and mind. Different Hindu schools take different positions: Advaita teaches atman IS Brahman; Dvaita teaches they are eternally distinct. The body dies; the atman does not.

Samsara: The Cycle of Birth and Death

Samsara is the continuing cycle through which the atman passes. When a body dies, the atman is reborn into a new body — human, animal or other form — determined by the accumulation of karma. This cycle is not understood as progress in a straight line but as a wheel that can turn endlessly.

In Birmingham, Deepa, a 45-year-old Shaivite Hindu, describes how the concept of samsara shapes her family’s approach to death: “When my mother died, we grieved, of course — but we also knew that her atman had moved on. The body returns to the earth but the soul continues its journey.” The concept of samsara does not trivialise death but places it within a much larger spiritual story.

Karma: Moral Action and Its Consequences

Karma literally means “action” but carries the specific meaning of the moral consequences of intentional actions. The law of karma teaches that every intentional action — physical, verbal or mental — generates consequences that must be experienced, in this life or in future lives.

A critical distinction for exam success: karma in Hinduism is not fate or destiny. It is moral causation — the result of a being’s own free choices. Because karma depends on intention, the tradition teaches that human beings have genuine free will. Acts performed with selfless intent, without attachment to the outcome, generate less binding karma than acts driven by desire or self-interest. This is the teaching of the Bhagavad Gita: perform your duty (dharma) without attachment to the fruits of the action.

Good karma — generated by righteous, selfless, compassionate action — leads the atman towards better conditions in future lives and ultimately towards liberation. Bad karma — generated by harmful, selfish actions — draws the atman back into difficult circumstances. The Bhagavad Gita teaches that devotion to God (bhakti) and the performance of one’s duty (dharma) without attachment are the highest ways to generate positive karma and progress towards liberation.

Students often describe karma as “what goes around comes around” or as predetermined fate. The Hindu teaching is more precise: karma is moral causation — actions have consequences, but those consequences unfold through a person’s own free choices. There is room for growth, purification and even divine grace. A person who has accumulated harmful karma through past actions is not trapped; through righteous action, devotion and wisdom they can change the trajectory of their atman’s journey. Examiners reward the distinction between karma as fate (incorrect) and karma as the moral law of consequences shaped by free will (correct).

Moksha is one of the four purusharthas (aims of human life), alongside dharma (ethical duty), artha (material prosperity) and kama (pleasure and love). A common exam misconception is that Hinduism treats worldly life negatively — that moksha means rejecting artha and kama altogether. The tradition teaches something more nuanced: artha and kama are legitimate and important aims, provided they are pursued within the bounds of dharma. Moksha is the ultimate destination, but for most Hindus in the householder stage of life, the focus is on dharma, artha and kama in a righteous balance. Moksha becomes the primary aim only in the later stages of life — particularly the renunciation stage (sannyasa). The Bhagavad Gita’s teaching on performing duty without attachment (nishkama karma) bridges the gap: by fulfilling dharma without clinging to its fruits, a person generates the positive karma that draws the atman closer to liberation, even while living a fully engaged worldly life.

Moksha: Liberation from Samsara

Moksha is the supreme goal of human existence: liberation from the cycle of samsara. When the atman achieves moksha, it is no longer reborn. Different schools describe moksha differently:

In Advaita Vedanta, moksha means the atman realising that it has always been identical to Brahman — the illusion of a separate self dissolves and the individual merges with the ultimate. In Vishishtadvaita, moksha means the atman entering into a state of eternal closeness with Vishnu, retaining its individual identity but dwelling in divine bliss. In Vaishnavite bhakti traditions, moksha is sometimes understood as eternal loving relationship with Krishna — a state of divine love rather than mere absorption.

The Bhagavad Gita teaches that the four paths of yoga (which are covered in the Practices unit) each offer routes towards moksha: through action (karma yoga), through knowledge (jnana yoga), through meditation (astanga yoga) and through devotion (bhakti yoga). The paths suit different temperaments but all lead towards liberation.

Personal Virtues and Responses to Suffering

Hindu teaching identifies specific virtues that support the journey towards moksha. Ahimsa (non-harm) is one of the most important: it shapes diet (many Hindus are vegetarian), professional choices and relationships. The Hindu tradition also emphasises respect, empathy, mind and sense control, humility and love (prema) as qualities that purify karma and bring the atman closer to liberation.

Suffering (dukkha-like experiences in Hindu terms) is understood through the lens of karma: suffering may result from past actions, may be an opportunity for spiritual growth, or may test and purify the soul. Ignorance (avidya) is considered the fundamental cause of samsara: the mistaken belief that the physical self is the real self perpetuates the cycle. Knowledge of the true nature of atman and Brahman — achieved through scripture, practice and the grace of God — is the path out.

Key Fact

Hindu personal virtues: ahimsa (non-harm), respect, empathy, mind/sense control, humility, love. All are understood as expressions of dharma and as ways of accumulating positive karma that supports progress towards moksha.
exam_tip_html:
The 6-mark Explain question may ask you to “Explain two Hindu beliefs about what happens after death.” Your go-to source is the Bhagavad Gita, which teaches that the atman is indestructible and that it passes from body to body through samsara until achieving moksha. Name the Bhagavad Gita, state the teaching, and develop your two reasons. Without a named source, your answer is capped below Mastering.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, you must reach a justified conclusion. If the statement is “Karma is the most important Hindu belief because it explains suffering,” you must weigh the arguments and say which side is stronger. Remember: do not describe karma as fate — distinguish it from fate by explaining it as moral causation through free will. This distinction earns credit on the mark scheme.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atman is the eternal inner self, distinct from the body and mind. It passes through samsara (the cycle of rebirth) driven by karma (the moral consequences of intentional actions). Karma is not fate — it is moral causation shaped by free will.
  • Moksha is liberation from samsara — the ultimate goal of Hindu life. Different schools describe it differently: Advaita teaches merging with Brahman; Vaishnavism teaches eternal love with Krishna. The Bhagavad Gita identifies devotion, action and knowledge as paths to liberation.
  • Key virtues — ahimsa, respect, humility, love — generate positive karma and support the atman’s journey. Ignorance (avidya) of the true self is the root cause of continued rebirth.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes karma in Hindu belief?
A) A fixed destiny decided by God before birth
B) The moral consequences of intentional actions across lifetimes
C) The inner self that passes from body to body at death
D) Liberation from the cycle of birth and death
practice_questions.marks: B) The moral consequences of intentional actions across lifetimes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: What is the Hindu term for the cycle of birth, death and rebirth?
Give two ways in which belief in karma might influence how a Hindu lives.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable content: a Hindu may practise ahimsa (non-harm) because harming others generates negative karma; a Hindu may perform duties selflessly (karma yoga) because the Bhagavad Gita teaches that action without attachment produces less binding karma; a Hindu may be vegetarian because ahimsa extends to animals; a Hindu may practise regular puja to accumulate good karma and purify past actions.

practice_questions.text:
Rohit is a 17-year-old Vaishnavite Hindu who has just started studying the Bhagavad Gita at his mandir in Leicester. He asks his teacher why the Gita says the atman cannot be destroyed.
Explain two Hindu beliefs about the nature of the atman.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable beliefs: the atman is eternal and cannot be destroyed (Bhagavad Gita teaching); the atman is distinct from the body and mind; the atman passes through samsara from body to body; the atman is ultimately related to or identical with Brahman (naming a school such as Advaita earns development credit).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Hindu beliefs about liberation (moksha).
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed beliefs about moksha with well-integrated source (e.g. Bhagavad Gita on performing duty without attachment as a path to liberation; Upanishadic teaching on atman and Brahman; naming Advaita Vedanta or Vaishnavism to show different understandings of what moksha means). Development uses 'because', 'this means that', 'as a result'. Secure: Two beliefs present, source referenced but partially developed. Developing: Beliefs stated without development; source absent or generic ('Hindu scripture'). Emerging: Basic description of samsara with no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in karma is the most important Hindu belief because it explains all suffering.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Karma provides a coherent explanation for why individuals experience different life circumstances; it offers a framework for understanding suffering as the result of past moral actions rather than random chance. It also motivates ethical behaviour — the knowledge that actions have consequences encourages righteous living. The Bhagavad Gita places karma at the centre of its teaching (karma yoga). Arguments against: Other Hindu beliefs are equally or more central: atman (the eternal self) and moksha (liberation) are the fundamental goals; Brahman as ultimate reality is the basis of all Hindu philosophy. The concept of divine grace (especially in Vaishnavism) suggests that liberation does not depend solely on karma — devotion to God (bhakti) can transcend accumulated karma. Many Hindus would say that ignorance (avidya), not karma itself, is the root cause of suffering. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that suffering is better explained through natural, social and economic causes than through metaphysical moral causation — and that understanding these causes is more likely to reduce suffering. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that karma is an important Hindu belief but not the only one; most Hindu traditions would place Brahman, atman and moksha as the foundational framework within which karma operates. The statement is therefore partly true but overstated. Mastering: Full range, sources named, sub-tradition contrast, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Basic description.

knowledge_checks.q: What is atman in Hindu belief?
options: The cycle of birth, death and rebirth
Liberation from the cycle of samsara
The eternal inner self, distinct from the body and mind
The moral consequences of actions across lifetimes

knowledge_checks.q: Which Hindu philosophical school teaches that atman and Brahman are ultimately identical?
Karma in Hinduism refers to the moral _____ of intentional actions.
The Hindu virtue of ahimsa means non-_____.
Match each Hindu concept to its correct description:
right: The cycle of birth, death and rebirth through which the atman passes
The law of moral causation — intentional actions produce consequences
Liberation from the cycle of samsara — the ultimate goal of human life

flashcard_questions.a: The eternal inner self, distinct from the body and mind, held to be divine in Hindu belief.
The cycle of birth, death and rebirth through which the atman passes until liberation.
The law of moral causation — intentional actions produce consequences affecting future lives.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is karma not the same as fate?
flashcard_questions.a: Karma depends on intentional free choices; a person can change their karmic trajectory through righteous action.
Liberation from samsara — the ultimate goal of Hindu life, achieved through devotion, knowledge or action.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Advaita Vedanta teach about moksha?
flashcard_questions.a: That moksha means realising that atman and Brahman are identical — the illusion of a separate self dissolves.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita teach about the atman?
flashcard_questions.a: That the atman is indestructible — it cannot be cut, burned, wetted or dried.
Non-violence or non-harm — one of the highest Hindu virtues, applied to all living beings.
Ignorance or spiritual blindness — the mistaken belief that the physical self is the true self.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Bhagavad Gita teach Hindus to reduce binding karma?
flashcard_questions.a: By performing duty (dharma) without attachment to the fruits of the action.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Dvaita school's teaching on atman and Brahman?
flashcard_questions.a: That atman and Brahman are eternally distinct — the soul depends on Brahman but never merges with it.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two personal virtues promoted by Hindu teaching on karma.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: ahimsa (non-harm), respect, humility, love (prema), empathy, mind/sense control.

glossary_terms.definition: The eternal inner self of an individual — distinct from the body and mind, held to be divine.
The cycle of birth, death and rebirth through which the atman passes until it achieves moksha.
The Hindu law of moral causation — intentional actions produce consequences across this and future lives.
Liberation from the cycle of samsara — the ultimate goal of human life in Hindu belief.
Non-violence or non-harm — a key Hindu virtue applied to thought, speech and action towards all beings.
Ignorance or spiritual blindness — the mistaken belief that the physical self is the true self.
A Hindu philosophical school teaching that atman and Brahman are ultimately identical.

hero_image_caption: The atman journeys through samsara until it achieves moksha — liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
